sections.text: In June of twenty seventeen, a team of eight researchers at Google posted a short paper with an unusually playful title: Attention Is All You Need. It described a new model for translating sentences, which they called the Transformer, and it quietly became the foundation for almost every large language model in use today. In the next few minutes we are going to read that paper together, from the problem it set out to solve, through each of its ideas, to the results that made the field take notice.

The task the authors cared about is called sequence transduction, which means turning one sequence into another, and the classic example is translating English into German. At the time, the best systems for this were recurrent neural networks. A recurrent network reads a sentence a little like reading through a keyhole, one word at a time, folding each new word into a single running summary called the hidden state. That design has two costs. The first is speed: every step has to wait for the one before it, so a long sentence cannot be spread across the thousands of cores in a modern graphics card. The second is memory: by the time the network reaches the end of a long sentence, what it knew about the beginning has been squeezed through every step in between, and it fades. Researchers had already found a partial remedy, a mechanism called attention, which lets the translator look back at every input word directly. But attention was always added on top of a recurrent network. This paper asks a simple question: what if attention were the whole model?

Here is the central idea. Think of a dictionary in a programming language, where you hand over a key and get back the value stored under it. Attention is a soft version of that lookup. Every word in the sentence produces three vectors: a query, which describes what the word is looking for, a key, which describes what it has to offer, and a value, which is the information it will pass along. To update one word, we compare its query with the key of every word, using a dot product, which is large when two vectors point in similar directions. A softmax turns those scores into weights that are positive and add up to one, and the word's new representation is the weighted average of all the values. Take a sentence the paper itself examines: the law will never be perfect, but its application should be just. Attention lets the word its draw its meaning from the word law, several words away, in a single step.

Because every word does this at the same time, the whole operation can be written with matrices. Stack the queries into a matrix Q, the keys into K and the values into V, and attention becomes the softmax of Q times K transpose, divided by the square root of d k, multiplied by V. That one line is the heart of the paper, and it is just two matrix multiplications and a softmax, exactly the kind of work graphics cards are built for. The division deserves a moment. The dot product of two random vectors grows with their dimension, and when the scores become large, the softmax turns extremely peaked, putting nearly all of its weight on a single word and passing back vanishing gradients during training. Dividing by the square root of the dimension keeps the scores in a range where the softmax stays soft. In the part of the model that writes the translation, one more detail matters: a mask hides the words that come later, so the model cannot peek at the answer while it learns to produce it.

A single attention pattern can only capture one kind of relationship at a time, so the authors run several side by side. They project the queries, keys and values into eight smaller subspaces, run attention separately in each, then join the results and project them back to full size. Each of these is called a head, and because every head works in a smaller space, eight of them cost about as much as one full-sized head. When the authors looked inside the trained model, they found that the heads had specialised. Some followed the grammatical structure of the sentence, while others, like the pair shown here from the paper, appear to work out which noun a pronoun refers to.

There is a catch in everything so far. Attention compares every word with every other word, but nothing in that comparison knows the order the words came in. Shuffle the sentence, and each word receives exactly the same weighted average, so dog bites man and man bites dog would look identical. The fix is to add a signal that encodes position to each word's vector before anything else happens. The authors used sine and cosine waves of many different frequencies, from very fast to very slow, so that every position receives its own distinctive pattern, rather like a clock with many hands turning at different speeds. This choice has a useful property: moving a fixed distance along the sentence corresponds to a simple linear transformation of the pattern, which makes relative positions easy for the model to learn.

Now we can assemble the whole machine, in the diagram most people remember from the paper. On the left is the encoder, which reads the input sentence. Each word becomes an embedding vector, plus its positional encoding, and then passes through a block with two parts: multi-head self-attention, where every word looks at every other word, and a small feed-forward network applied to each word on its own. Around each part sits a residual connection, which adds the input back to the output, followed by layer normalisation, and together they help a deep network train stably. The encoder stacks six of these blocks. On the right is the decoder, which writes the translation one word at a time. Its blocks have three parts: masked self-attention over the words written so far, then cross-attention, whose queries come from the decoder while its keys and values come from the encoder, which is how the translation consults the original sentence, and finally the same feed-forward network. At the top, a linear layer and a softmax turn the result into a probability for every word in the vocabulary.

The paper makes its case for this design with a short table comparing kinds of layers. In a recurrent layer, the number of steps that must happen one after another grows with the length of the sentence, and a signal travelling between two distant words has to pass through every word in between. A self-attention layer connects every pair of words directly, so the path between any two positions has length one, and all of the work can happen at once. The price is that comparing every word with every other word grows with the square of the sentence length. But for sentences of ordinary length, which are shorter than the vectors that represent each word, self-attention turns out to be cheaper per layer as well.

The authors trained on the standard English to German and English to French translation benchmarks, using a single machine with eight graphics cards. The base model trained for about twelve hours, and the larger model for three and a half days, which was still a small fraction of the computation spent on the best earlier systems. A few of their training choices became standard practice: a learning rate that warms up before it decays, dropout, and label smoothing, which teaches the model to be slightly less certain of its answers. The results were striking. On English to German, the big Transformer scored twenty eight point four BLEU, more than two points above the best previous results, including ensembles of several models combined. On English to French it set a new single-model record of forty one point eight. And to show that the architecture was not specific to translation, the authors also applied it to parsing the grammatical structure of English sentences, where it performed surprisingly well.

The paper's conclusion is modest. The authors write that they are excited about the future of attention-based models, and that they plan to apply them to images, audio and video. That turned out to be an understatement. Within about a year, the first GPT model was built from the Transformer's decoder, and BERT from its encoder. Vision transformers applied the same blocks to patches of images, and attention became a central part of systems from protein structure prediction to the language models people now use every day. Most of what made that possible is already in this short paper: a single operation that lets every word look at every other word at once, simple enough to grow with the hardware that was arriving to run it.
